Agent Foundations

Cluster DD.4.1 · Agent Foundations

Superintelligence alignment may allow only one critical try, with no trial and error on a system more capable than anything yet observed. Agent foundations seeks research directions that survive extreme optimization and self-modification.

By Daniel C, Satya Benson (Williams College)

What you’ll learn

(What.) By the end of the day, students can explain embedded agency: why an agent built into the world it acts on (made of the same stuff, smaller than its environment, with no clean input/output boundary, able to model and modify itself) breaks the standard dualistic picture. For each of the day's core research directions (called 'strands') they can state the central problem and a plain-language description of a main result: the complete class theorem (consequentialist foundations), Löb's theorem and the tiling obstacle (self-modification), the logical-induction criterion (logical uncertainty), optimization as local entropy reduction (optimization and thermodynamics), and selection theorems (descriptive agent foundations). They can describe at last one strand in mathematical detail. They can explain how each strand is an offshoot of the central threads reflective stability and embedded agency.

(Why.) Aligning a superintelligence is a problem we may have to get right on the first critical try, reasoning about a system more capable than anything we have observed, before it exists. That rules out pure trial and error and demands concepts that stay meaningful under extreme optimization pressure and self-modification. Agent foundations supplies (or tries to supply) those concepts, and this day gives students a map of some main research directions and how they fit together.

(How.) Each student goes deep on one pre-reading track beforehand. A one-hour morning lecture lays out the main threads (reflective stability and embedded agency) and previews every strand. Students then read the shared fundamental readings and, in small groups mixing different tracks, run cross-pollination discussions that connect their topics to embedded agency. The afternoon makes a few results rigorous through exercises.

1. Prerequisites

  • Comfort with elementary discrete probability (random variables, expectation, conditional probability).
  • Basic formal logic (provability, quantifiers) and basic computability (programs, halting); needed for the Löb and logical-induction strands.
  • Basic information theory (entropy, mutual information); needed for the optimization strand.
  • No prior agent-foundations background is assumed; every term used on the day is introduced on the day or in the readings. An introductory overview of the AI alignment problem (as in the intro-alignment module) is helpful context but not required.
  • Provided refresher notes cover the gaps: a probability theory refresher, a formal logic refresher, a computability theory refresher, and an information theory, causality, and statistical mechanics refresher. Point students at the one matching their weakest area before the day.

2. Content

Exercise sheet: Section 3 below, with worked solutions. The lecture deck is built from this module's own slides.tex and linked at the top of the page.

2.1 Fast-track

To get the core in about an hour, or to catch up after missing the day:

  • Read the "Morning lecture" summary below for the unifying spine (reflective stability, embedded agency, the modelling-vs-implementation split).
  • Read Embedded agency up to and including section 3.3, then section 4.1, and Why agent foundations in full.
  • Pick the one strand closest to your background from "The five strands" below and read its first (most conceptual) listed reading.
  • Skim the takeaways at the end of each strand summary.

2.2 Main content

Agent foundations is not one theory but several research strands (research directions), each attacking a different facet of the same problem: how to reason about, and build, stable agents that are embedded in the world they act on. This day is organized around five such strands (consequentialist foundations; Löb's theorem and tiling agents; logical induction; optimization and thermodynamics; descriptive agent foundations). Each student pre-reads one strand in depth before the day; the morning lecture supplies the spine that connects them; the shared fundamental readings and a small-group discussion knit them into a single picture; and an exercise session makes a few of the results rigorous.

Read top to bottom, this section runs: the unifying threads (the morning lecture), then the fundamental readings that give a bird's-eye view, then the five strands each with its readings, then the cross-pollination discussion, the exercises, and a self-check.

2.2.1 Morning lecture

  • Why agent foundations. We may need key safety properties to hold on the first critical try, for an agent far more capable than any we can study directly. Agent foundations looks for the properties capable agents share in general, so we can reason about them in advance.
  • Reflective stability. A safety property only matters if it survives the agent's own self-modification: a capable agent may rewrite its code, build a more capable successor, or revise its world model. A property is reflectively stable if it is invariant under all of these. Working assumption: under enough optimization pressure, a property persists only if there is some reason it must. Reflective stability is the thread running through every strand.
  • Robust concepts ("true names"). Goodhart's law says a proxy that becomes a target stops measuring what we want. So a theory of agency must be built from concepts that do not break under optimization, the "true names" of optimization, goals, world models, and embeddedness.
  • Two pathways of impact (following C. Wyeth). Modelling: build an abstract mathematical model of an idealised capable agent and use it to show why a given alignment proposal would fail. Implementation: develop a theory far enough to build and inspect an actual system, often favouring a modular architecture (a separate, inspectable world model, planner, and goal) so each part can be checked.
  • Dualistic vs embedded agents. The standard picture (an agent with clean I/O, "larger than" and "outside" its environment, holding a full world model in its head) is dualistic. A real agent is embedded: part of the world, made of the same pieces, smaller than its environment, with no crisp boundary, and able to be copied, modified, or to model itself. Embeddedness is what makes self-improvement, multi-agent reasoning about copies, and self-reference unavoidable, and it is what the rest of the day is about.

2.2.2 Fundamental reading

  • Embedded agency: read up to and including section 3.3, then section 4.1. The canonical statement of the embedded-agency problem cluster (the Alexei/Emmy framing the lecture uses).
  • Why agent foundations: read entirely. Why this abstract, theory-first approach is worth pursuing.
  • Reflectively consistent degree of freedom: read entirely. The precise notion behind a property an agent would not self-modify away, which is the day's recurring theme of reflective stability.
  • General purpose search: read entirely. Why a capable mind plausibly contains a retargetable search process.

2.2.3 The five strands (pre-reading tracks)

The five strands are different facets of one problem, embedded agency; each student pre-reads one. Every summary below is self-contained at the conceptual level and ends with that strand's readings (start with the first listed, which is the most conceptual). The morning lecture previews all five; the cross-pollination discussion connects them.

1. Consequentialist foundations. If an agent's preferences are cyclic, an adversary can money-pump it through trades that each look acceptable but leave it strictly worse off. So any agent that reliably avoids such dominated strategies behaves as if it maximizes a utility function. The complete class theorem sharpens this: any decision rule that is not dominated (Pareto-optimal across environments) is Bayes-optimal under some prior with full support. This is representational, not mechanistic: it says a capable, non-self-defeating agent looks like a Bayesian expected-utility maximizer from the outside, without saying it has a utility function inside, and without telling us which utility function (the hard part). Takeaway: coherence gives a reflectively-stable target (a dominated strategy is one a rational agent would self-modify away from), but it under-determines the agent's actual goals. Readings: Coherent decisions imply consistent utilities (Introduction; "Why not circular preferences?"; "Probabilities and expected utilities" through "Conditional probability"; Conclusion); The measuring stick of utility; Complete class: consequentialist foundations.

2. Löb's theorem and tiling agents. A capable agent may build a successor more capable than itself. By Vingean reflection, it cannot verify the successor by simulating it (if it could predict the successor's exact moves, it would be that capable already), so it must reason abstractly about the successor's design. The natural strategy ("trust the successor because it only takes actions it has proved safe") needs the parent to trust the successor's proofs. Löb's theorem blocks this: if a consistent system L can prove "if L proves C then C", then L already proves C. A consistent system cannot vouch for its own proofs in the abstract, only for a strictly weaker system's. So a naive chain of self-improvements uses an ever-weaker proof system (a "telomere" of logical strength that runs out), the finite descent problem. The tiling-agents programme studies whether this obstacle can be overcome. Takeaway: self-trust under self-modification is not free; it runs straight into a logical wall. Readings: Introduction to Löb's theorem (up to and including section 3); Vingean reflection; Walkthrough of the tiling agents paper (start through "Finite Descent Problem", then "What self-modifying agents need").

3. Logical induction. Standard Bayesian reasoning assumes logical omniscience: the agent instantly knows all consequences of its beliefs. A bounded agent cannot (it may know a program's source yet not its output, or the axioms yet not whether a number is prime). Logical induction (Garrabrant et al.) handles this by picturing a market that prices logical sentences in [0,1]; the logical-induction criterion requires only that no efficient (polynomial-time) trader can exploit the market for unbounded profit, a computable weakening of the Dutch-book argument. That single condition yields convergence and coherence in the limit, timely learning of statistical patterns (it prices "the nth digit of pi is 7" near 1/10 without computing it), and self-trust (current credence equals a weighted average of expected future credences). Takeaway: a principled model of how a bounded agent should hold probabilities over facts it has not yet computed. Readings: An intuitive guide to Garrabrant induction; Logical induction (chapters 1 and 3; skim chapter 4).

4. Optimization and thermodynamics. A powerful agent reliably steers the world into a narrow region of outcomes, ones extremely unlikely under any random process. This is local entropy reduction: concentrating probability mass from a broad initial distribution onto a narrow target. Even a pure predictor has an objective reason to attend to optimizers: naming what an optimizer steers toward predicts the outcome cheaply and robustly, where modelling the initial conditions would be expensive and chaos-fragile. Steering is bounded by information: the Touchette-Lloyd inequality says the entropy reduction a sighted agent achieves over a blind baseline is at most the mutual information between its observations and actions (ΔH≤ΔHblindmax⁡+I(X;A)\Delta H \leq \Delta H_{\text{blind}}^{\max}+ I(X;A)ΔH≤ΔHblindmax​+I(X;A)). Algorithmic thermodynamics (Ebtekar and Hutter) replaces ensemble entropy with Kolmogorov complexity, giving laws for individual states and making an embedded agent's knowledge an endogenous physical quantity (algorithmic mutual information between memory and environment), which is exactly its budget for optimization. Takeaway: optimization is physically constrained, and "knowing more" formally means "being able to optimize more." Readings: the self-contained note Optimization and thermodynamics (read entirely; appendix optional) is the primary reading; its underlying sources are The ground of optimization (up to and including "Relationship to Garrabrant and Demski's Embedded Agency"), Generalized heat engine, and Algorithmic thermodynamics and three types of optimization.

5. Descriptive agent foundations. Normative agent foundations asks what an ideal agent should look like; descriptive asks what agents actually arising in the world (bacteria, neural networks, future AI) look like, and aims to read off their goals, world model, and decision structure from the outside. It works bottom-up from properties of the world (modularity, selection pressures, computational limits). Selection theorems aim to prove results of the form "any system selected to achieve goal G in environment E must contain structure approximately isomorphic to X", giving mechanistic rather than merely representational accounts of agency. A key example: the world's modularity (it decomposes into sparsely-interacting subsystems) is what makes both world-modelling (Bayesian networks propagate updates locally) and planning (general-purpose search can pursue decoupled subgoals) tractable. Takeaway: the complementary direction to coherence: not "non-dominated agents can be described as maximizers" but "what pressures make agent-like structure actually arise." Readings: Selection theorems: a program for understanding agents; How we picture Bayesian agents; What selection theorems do we expect/want.

2.2.4 Cross-pollination discussion

On the day, students who pre-read different strands meet in small mixed groups and work to connect their topics into one picture of embedded agency: how a logical inductor's trust in its future self relates to a tiling agent's trust in its successor, how the coherence account of goals relates to the thermodynamic one, how the representational view of agency (coherence) relates to the mechanistic one (selection theorems). The specific discussion prompts used are listed in the teaching guide.

2.2.5 Exercise session

Five exercises (full statements and worked solutions in Section 3), grouped by topic:

Logical uncertainty and self-reference.

  • Exercise 1: Gödel's second incompleteness theorem (difficulty 4/5, importance 4/5). Via a self-referential program: a Gödel sentence is true, a consistent system cannot prove its own consistency, and this is exactly the Löbian obstacle to self-trust. Parts (a) true Gödel sentence, (b) no self-consistency proof, (c) the obstacle.
  • Exercise 2: Löb's theorem (difficulty 3/5, importance 5/5). The three provability properties (necessitation, distribution, the Löb condition), a full proof of the theorem, and an application: FairBot programs cooperate by Löb's theorem. Parts (a-b) properties, (c-d) the proof, (e) FairBot.

Coherence and consequentialism.

  • Exercise 3: The complete class theorem (difficulty 3/5, importance 5/5). The equivalence between non-dominated strategies and Bayesian expected-utility maximization, via a geometric argument over the convex set of attainable reward vectors. Parts (a) admissibility, (b) faces and difference vectors, (c) constructing the rationalizing prior.

Descriptive agent foundations.

  • Exercise 4: The do-divergence theorem (difficulty 2/5, importance 4/5). Formalizes optimization as outcome concentration and proves that how far an agent can steer outcomes (a KL divergence from the unsteered baseline) is bounded by the mutual information between its observations and actions. The single-step backbone of the Touchette-Lloyd picture.
  • Exercise 5: Channel additivity (difficulty 3/5, importance 3/5). Optimal input distributions over independent channels: mutual information decomposes across channels, independence improves throughput, and an optimal policy need not coordinate across a modular environment (connecting modularity to tractable optimization).

2.3 Learn more

The readings for each strand are linked under that strand in the Main content above. Beyond them:

Algorithmic thermodynamics (Ebtekar). Foundations of algorithmic thermodynamics; Modelling the arrows of time with causal multibaker maps; Long-time derivation of the Boltzmann equation from hard-sphere dynamics.

Embedded and universal AI (Wyeth). Limit-computable grains of truth; Embeddedness failures in universal artificial intelligence; Value under ignorance.

Other directions. Introduction to the infra-Bayesianism sequence (non-realizable environments); The learning-theoretic agenda; Optimization at a distance; the hard problem of corrigibility and a critique of the corrigibility basin of attraction; the original tiling agents draft; and background notes on admissibility and the complete class theorem and the Dutch book argument.

Research frontier. The agent structure problem (whether strong optimization provably entails an internal world model), embedded variants of AIXI, and resource-theoretic accounts of instrumental convergence.

3. Exercises

The following are exercises on agent foundations. Each problem is broken into a sequence of lemmas leading to a main theorem. For each subquestion, try to prove the stated lemma before reading on. If you get stuck, you may treat the lemma as given and proceed to the next part.

Before diving into a formal derivation, try to build an intuition for why the statement should be true. Even if you don't complete the proof, having a clear intuitive picture of what's going on is more valuable than a mechanical derivation you don't understand. Don't worry if some of the terminology is unfamiliar — the exercises are designed to be self-contained, and it should be possible to follow the questions from context.

Formal systems and programs. A formal system is a precise set of rules for deriving mathematical statements from axioms. Fix a formal system LLL that is powerful enough to reason about programs (for instance, it can express statements about arithmetic, and any program can be encoded as a mathematical object that LLL can talk about). We write L⊢φL \vdash \varphiL⊢φ to mean that the statement φ\varphiφ is provable in LLL, i.e. there exists a finite sequence of steps, each justified by the rules of LLL, that derives φ\varphiφ.

We say LLL is consistent if it never proves a contradiction. We write ⊥\bot⊥ for a fixed contradictory statement (such as 0=10 = 10=1), so consistency means L⊬⊥L \nvdash \botL⊬⊥. We assume throughout that LLL is consistent.

Programs. By a program we mean a mechanical procedure that follows a fixed list of instructions. A program may halt (finish and produce an output) or run forever (keep executing without ever stopping). Since LLL can reason about programs, it can express the statement "program MMM halts", which we write as Halts(M)\mathsf{Halts}(M)Halts(M).

The bridge between LLL and programs. Formal systems and programs are intimately connected, and the key to these exercises is switching back and forth between the two perspectives:

  • From programs to LLL (concrete outputs become proofs). If a program concretely produces an output (e.g. it halts after some number of steps, or it finds a string with a certain property), then LLL can verify this by tracing through the execution step by step. In particular: if a program actually halts, then LLL can prove that it halts.
  • From LLL to programs (proofs can be found by search). Proofs in LLL are finite strings that can be checked mechanically. So for any statement PPP, we can write a program that searches through all possible strings, checks whether each one is a valid LLL-proof of PPP, and halts if it finds one:
ProofSeeker(P)  :=  “try every string; halt iff one is a valid L-proof of P.”\texttt{ProofSeeker}(P) \;:=\; \text{``try every string; halt iff one is a valid $L$-proof of $P$.''}ProofSeeker(P):=“try every string; halt iff one is a valid L-proof of P.”

This program halts if and only if PPP is provable in LLL.

Whenever you derive a fact about LLL (e.g. that some statement is or isn't provable), ask what that implies for the corresponding proof-search program, and vice versa.

The provability predicate □P\Box P□P. We write □P\Box P□P for the statement, expressed within LLL itself, that "PPP is provable in LLL." This is a genuine mathematical statement that LLL can reason about, because it is equivalent to the claim that ProofSeeker(P)\texttt{ProofSeeker}(P)ProofSeeker(P) halts, and LLL can talk about programs.

The crucial distinction is between L⊢PL \vdash PL⊢P and L⊢□PL \vdash \Box PL⊢□P:

  • L⊢PL \vdash PL⊢P means that PPP is provable: there exists a concrete proof of PPP in LLL. This is a fact about LLL that we observe from the outside.
  • L⊢□PL \vdash \Box PL⊢□P means that LLL has proved a statement about itself: namely, that a proof of PPP exists (equivalently, that ProofSeeker(P)\texttt{ProofSeeker}(P)ProofSeeker(P) halts). But this is a claim LLL is making about the ProofSeeker(P)\texttt{ProofSeeker}(P)ProofSeeker(P) program, not a direct certificate for PPP.

Intuition. To see why L⊢PL \vdash PL⊢P and L⊢□PL \vdash \Box PL⊢□P are conceptually distinct, consider the two different ways LLL might prove that ProofSeeker(P)\texttt{ProofSeeker}(P)ProofSeeker(P) halts. The first is to actually trace through its execution: if it halts after, say, a million steps, LLL can verify this step by step, and the proof that ProofSeeker(P)\texttt{ProofSeeker}(P)ProofSeeker(P) found along the way is itself a direct LLL-proof of PPP. In this case, L⊢□PL \vdash \Box PL⊢□P and L⊢PL \vdash PL⊢P seems to come hand in hand. But there is a second way: LLL might reason abstractly about the program's behaviour without ever simulating it. (This is analogous to how you might argue that a sorting algorithm must eventually finish without tracing through every swap it makes.) Such a proof establishes that ProofSeeker(P)\texttt{ProofSeeker}(P)ProofSeeker(P) halts — and therefore that some proof of PPP exists — but the proof itself is about the program, not about PPP. It need not contain, or even hint at, what the actual proof of PPP looks like. This is the gap that LLL cannot close in general: knowing abstractly that a proof is "out there" is not the same as having the proof in hand.

What "provable in LLL" means (and what it does not). It is important to distinguish between being convinced that something is true and proving it in LLL. When we say "LLL can carry out this argument" or "LLL proves PPP," we do not mean that a reasonable person reading the argument would find it convincing. We mean something much more specific: that there exists a sequence of formulas, each of which is either an axiom of LLL or follows from earlier formulas by one of LLL's explicitly listed inference rules, and whose last line is PPP. The formal system LLL is a machine: it has no understanding, no intuition, and no ability to say "well, this obviously follows." Every single step must be justified by a specific rule.

From the outside, we can see that if ProofSeeker(P)\texttt{ProofSeeker}(P)ProofSeeker(P) halts then a proof of PPP exists, so PPP is provable. But can LLL carry out this reasoning internally, always concluding PPP from □P\Box P□P? Lob's theorem (Exercise 2) shows that the answer is no: any consistent LLL that derives PPP from □P\Box P□P for all PPP is in fact inconsistent.

Exercise 3.1 (Godel's second incompleteness theorem). Key fact. If a program MMM actually halts (say, after 17 steps), then LLL can verify this by checking the execution step by step, so L⊢Halts(M)L \vdash \mathsf{Halts}(M)L⊢Halts(M). However, if MMM runs forever, LLL cannot necessarily prove ¬Halts(M)\neg\mathsf{Halts}(M)¬Halts(M). (Informally: it is easy to certify that something stops, because you just exhibit the stopping point; but certifying that something runs forever is much harder, because you cannot check infinitely many steps.)

In fact, no consistent formal system can correctly settle the question "does MMM halt?" for every program MMM. To see why: if LLL could do this, we could write a program that, given any MMM, searches for an LLL-proof of either Halts(M)\mathsf{Halts}(M)Halts(M) or ¬Halts(M)\neg\mathsf{Halts}(M)¬Halts(M). Since LLL is assumed to settle every case, this search would always find a proof and halt, giving us a mechanical procedure that decides whether any program halts. But such a procedure cannot exist (this is the undecidability of the halting problem, a fundamental result in computer science that we take as given here).

A self-referencing program. It is possible to write programs that refer to their own source code. (As a simple example, a program can carry its own source code as a string and then operate on it.) Using this idea, define the following program:

Z(A)  :=  “search for an L-proof of ¬Halts(A(A)); halt if one is found.”Z(A) \;:=\; \text{``search for an $L$-proof of $\neg\mathsf{Halts}(A(A))$; halt if one is found.''}Z(A):=“search for an L-proof of ¬Halts(A(A)); halt if one is found.”

Here A(A)A(A)A(A) means "run program AAA with its own source code as input." So Z(A)Z(A)Z(A) searches for a proof that the program AAA-run-on-itself runs forever.

Now consider feeding ZZZ its own source code. The program Z(Z)Z(Z)Z(Z) searches for an LLL-proof that Z(Z)Z(Z)Z(Z) runs forever. Define the statement:

G  :=  ¬Halts(Z(Z)).G \;:=\; \neg\mathsf{Halts}(Z(Z)).G:=¬Halts(Z(Z)).

In words: GGG says "Z(Z)Z(Z)Z(Z) runs forever." Notice the self-referential structure: Z(Z)Z(Z)Z(Z) halts if and only if it finds an LLL-proof of GGG (i.e. a proof that Z(Z)Z(Z)Z(Z) runs forever).

Part 1(a). Show that GGG is true, assuming LLL is consistent.

Hint: Consider two cases. Either Z(Z)Z(Z)Z(Z) halts or it doesn't. In each case, use the bridge between programs and LLL (if a program halts, LLL can prove it; if LLL proves something, the corresponding proof-search program finds that proof and halts) to derive what follows. One of the two cases leads to a contradiction with the consistency of LLL.

Part 1(b). Show that if LLL can prove its own consistency (i.e. L⊢¬□⊥L \vdash \neg\Box\botL⊢¬□⊥), then LLL is in fact inconsistent.

Hint: In Part 1(a), you argued from outside LLL that GGG is true, and the argument used only one assumption about LLL: that LLL is consistent. If LLL can prove its own consistency, then every step of your outside argument can be carried out inside LLL as a formal derivation. What would LLL then be able to prove? And what would the corresponding program do?

Part 1(c). Suppose LLL can vouch for all of its own proofs, meaning L⊢□P→PL \vdash \Box P \to PL⊢□P→P for every statement PPP. (Read this as: "whenever LLL can prove PPP, then PPP is actually true," and LLL itself asserts this.) Show that LLL is inconsistent, in two steps:

  • (i) First, show that LLL proves it never proves anything false. That is: for any PPP with L⊢¬PL \vdash \neg PL⊢¬P, show that L⊢¬□PL \vdash \neg\Box PL⊢¬□P. Hint: The statement "if AAA then BBB" is logically equivalent to "if not BBB then not AAA". Apply this to □P→P\Box P \to P□P→P.
  • (ii) Apply (i) with P=⊥P = \botP=⊥, using the fact that ¬⊥\neg\bot¬⊥ ("a contradiction is false") is a tautology. Conclude that L⊢¬□⊥L \vdash \neg\Box\botL⊢¬□⊥, and use Part 1(b) to finish.

Remark (Self-trust, tiling agents, and the Lobian obstacle).

Any sufficiently advanced AI may eventually be able to modify its own code or build a successor system more capable than itself. But this raises a subtle problem. If the successor is genuinely smarter, the original agent cannot predict exactly what it will do — just as the programmers of a chess engine can reason that their program is "trying to win" without knowing its exact moves. So the original agent cannot verify its successor's safety by simulating it move by move. Instead, it must reason abstractly about the successor's design: "whatever my successor does, it will only take actions that it has proved lead to good outcomes."

This reasoning strategy is called tiling: the parent agent A1A_{1}A1​ builds a child agent A0A_{0}A0​, and wants to conclude not merely that A0A_{0}A0​ will only take actions that A0A_{0}A0​ has proved to be safe, but that those actions actually are safe. After all, A1A_{1}A1​ can verify from A0A_{0}A0​'s source code that A0A_{0}A0​ says "only take action xxx if I can prove that xxx leads to good outcomes." But this only tells A1A_{1}A1​ that A0A_{0}A0​ acts on what A0A_{0}A0​'s proof system certifies — it does not yet tell A1A_{1}A1​ that what A0A_{0}A0​'s proof system certifies is actually true. To close this gap, A1A_{1}A1​ needs to be able to prove, within its own reasoning, that A0A_{0}A0​'s proof system is sound: whenever A0A_{0}A0​'s system proves PPP, then PPP is actually true. When both agents use the same formal system LLL, this amounts to L⊢□P→PL \vdash \Box P \to PL⊢□P→P for all PPP.

Part 1(c) shows this is impossible: any consistent system that asserts □P→P\Box P \to P□P→P for all PPP is already inconsistent. A consistent system cannot vouch for its own proofs in the abstract — it can only trust a proof once it has witnessed it directly. This is the Lobian obstacle: the barrier created by Lob's theorem to self-trusting formal reasoning.

One might hope to work around this by having the parent use a stronger proof system than the child: a stronger system can trust a weaker one's proofs. But this means each successive agent in a chain of self-improvements must use a strictly weaker proof system than its predecessor, resulting in a "telomere" of logical strength that shortens with each generation. Eventually the chain runs out of trust. The tiling agents research programme studies how (and whether) this obstacle can be overcome, seeking agent architectures that can undergo indefinite self-improvement without their reasoning guarantees degrading at each step.

Solution

Recall Z(A)Z(A)Z(A) searches for an LLL-proof of ¬Halts(A(A))\neg\Halts(A(A))¬Halts(A(A)) and halts if it finds one, and

G  :=  ¬Halts(Z(Z)).G \;:=\; \neg\Halts(Z(Z)).G:=¬Halts(Z(Z)).

By construction Z(Z)Z(Z)Z(Z) searches for an LLL-proof of GGG, so

Z(Z) halts  ⟺  L⊢G.(⋆)Z(Z)\text{ halts}\iff L\proves G. \tag{$\star$}Z(Z) halts⟺L⊢G.(⋆)

Part 1(a). GGG is true (assuming LLL consistent).

Solution. Two cases.

  • Z(Z)Z(Z)Z(Z) halts. By (⋆\star ⋆), L⊢GL\proves GL⊢G, i.e. L⊢¬Halts(Z(Z))L\proves\neg\Halts(Z(Z))L⊢¬Halts(Z(Z)). But Z(Z)Z(Z)Z(Z) actually halts, so by the bridge L⊢Halts(Z(Z))L\proves\Halts(Z(Z))L⊢Halts(Z(Z)). Then LLL proves both Halts(Z(Z))\Halts(Z(Z))Halts(Z(Z)) and its negation, contradicting consistency.
  • Z(Z)Z(Z)Z(Z) runs forever. Then ¬Halts(Z(Z))\neg\Halts(Z(Z))¬Halts(Z(Z)), i.e. GGG, is true.

Consistency rules out the first case, so Z(Z)Z(Z)Z(Z) runs forever and GGG is true. □\square□

Part 1(b). If L⊢¬□KL\proves\neg\bx KL⊢¬□K (i.e. LLL proves its own consistency) then LLL is inconsistent.

Solution. The argument of 1(a) used only the consistency of LLL, and each step is a finite manipulation of programs and proofs that LLL can formalize. Reading it inside LLL: "Z(Z)Z(Z)Z(Z) halts" yields □G\bx G□G (by construction) and □Halts(Z(Z))\bx\Halts(Z(Z))□Halts(Z(Z)) (the bridge), hence □K\bx K□K; contrapositively L⊢¬□K→GL\proves \neg\bx K \to GL⊢¬□K→G. If L⊢¬□KL\proves\neg\bx KL⊢¬□K, modus ponens gives

L⊢G,i.e.L⊢¬Halts(Z(Z)).L\proves G,\qquad\text{i.e.}\qquad L\proves\neg\Halts(Z(Z)).L⊢G,i.e.L⊢¬Halts(Z(Z)).

But L⊢GL\proves GL⊢G means Z(Z)Z(Z)Z(Z)'s search finds a proof of GGG, so Z(Z)Z(Z)Z(Z) halts; by the bridge L⊢Halts(Z(Z))L\proves\Halts(Z(Z))L⊢Halts(Z(Z)). Now LLL proves both Halts(Z(Z))\Halts(Z(Z))Halts(Z(Z)) and ¬Halts(Z(Z))\neg\Halts(Z(Z))¬Halts(Z(Z)), so LLL is inconsistent. □\square□

Part 1(c). If L⊢□P→PL\proves \bx P\to PL⊢□P→P for every PPP, then LLL is inconsistent.

Solution. (i) Fix PPP with L⊢¬PL\proves\neg PL⊢¬P. The contrapositive of □P→P\bx P\to P□P→P is ¬P→¬□P\neg P\to\neg\bx P¬P→¬□P, so from L⊢□P→PL\proves\bx P\to PL⊢□P→P we get L⊢¬P→¬□PL\proves\neg P\to\neg\bx PL⊢¬P→¬□P. With L⊢¬PL\proves\neg PL⊢¬P, modus ponens gives L⊢¬□PL\proves\neg\bx PL⊢¬□P.

(ii) Take P=KP=KP=K. Since ¬K\neg K¬K is a tautology, L⊢¬KL\proves\neg KL⊢¬K, so by (i) L⊢¬□KL\proves\neg\bx KL⊢¬□K. Thus LLL proves its own consistency, and Part 1(b) makes LLL inconsistent. □\square□

Exercise 3.2 (Lob's theorem). Lob's theorem says: if L⊢□C→CL \vdash \Box C \to CL⊢□C→C (i.e. LLL can prove "if CCC is provable then CCC is true"), then L⊢CL \vdash CL⊢C (i.e. CCC is already provable in LLL). In other words, the only statements for which LLL can close the gap between "provably provable" and "provable" are the ones that were already provable to begin with.

The proof uses three properties of the provability predicate □\Box□. We state them here together with informal explanations of what they say about the proof-search program ProofSeeker\texttt{ProofSeeker}ProofSeeker.

(N)Necessitation.If L⊢φL \vdash \varphiL⊢φ then L⊢□φL \vdash \Box\varphiL⊢□φ.
(K)Distribution.L⊢□(φ→ψ)→(□φ→□ψ)L \vdash \Box(\varphi \to \psi) \to (\Box\varphi \to \Box\psi)L⊢□(φ→ψ)→(□φ→□ψ).
(4)Lob condition.L⊢□φ→□□φL \vdash \Box\varphi \to \Box\Box\varphiL⊢□φ→□□φ.

Part 2(a). Understanding Necessitation. Necessitation says: if φ\varphiφ is provable in LLL, then LLL can prove that φ\varphiφ is provable. Explain why this is true from the perspective of ProofSeeker\texttt{ProofSeeker}ProofSeeker.

Hint: If a proof of φ\varphiφ exists, then ProofSeeker(φ)\texttt{ProofSeeker}(\varphi)ProofSeeker(φ) will find it and halt.

Part 2(b). Understanding Distribution. It is helpful to think of a proof of φ→ψ\varphi \to \psiφ→ψ by analogy with a function: given any proof of φ\varphiφ as input, one can mechanically produce a proof of ψ\psiψ as output (by writing down the proof of φ\varphiφ, attaching the proof of φ→ψ\varphi \to \psiφ→ψ, and applying the logical rule that from φ\varphiφ and φ→ψ\varphi \to \psiφ→ψ one may conclude ψ\psiψ).

With this analogy, □(φ→ψ)\Box(\varphi \to \psi)□(φ→ψ) says that LLL has proved such a "proof-transforming function" exists. Distribution then says: if LLL knows that a function from φ\varphiφ-proofs to ψ\psiψ-proofs exists, and LLL knows that a φ\varphiφ-proof exists, then LLL can conclude that a ψ\psiψ-proof exists.

Explain why Distribution is true from the perspective of ProofSeeker\texttt{ProofSeeker}ProofSeeker.

Hint: If both ProofSeeker(φ→ψ)\texttt{ProofSeeker}(\varphi \to \psi)ProofSeeker(φ→ψ) and ProofSeeker(φ)\texttt{ProofSeeker}(\varphi)ProofSeeker(φ) halt, what can you do with their outputs? How can LLL deduce that ProofSeeker(ψ)\texttt{ProofSeeker}(\psi)ProofSeeker(ψ) halts?

We now prove Lob's theorem. The key ingredient is a self-referential sentence constructed using the same idea as in Exercise 1 (a sentence that talks about its own provability). Specifically, there exists a sentence λ\lambdaλ such that

L⊢λ  ↔  (□λ→C).L \vdash \lambda \;\leftrightarrow\; (\Box\lambda \to C).L⊢λ↔(□λ→C).

In words: λ\lambdaλ says "if I am provable, then CCC is true." (The existence of such a sentence is guaranteed by the same self-referential construction used to build GGG in Exercise 1; we take it as given here.)

Part 2(c). Show that L⊢□λ→□CL \vdash \Box\lambda \to \Box CL⊢□λ→□C.

Hint: The Lob sentence says L⊢λ→(□λ→C)L \vdash \lambda \to (\Box\lambda \to C)L⊢λ→(□λ→C). Apply Necessitation to get this fact inside a □\Box□, then use Distribution twice (once to "unwrap" the outer implication, once to handle □λ→C\Box\lambda \to C□λ→C inside). Use the Lob condition to handle the resulting □□λ\Box\Box\lambda□□λ.

Part 2(d). Now assume L⊢□C→CL \vdash \Box C \to CL⊢□C→C. Using Part 2(c) and the Lob sentence, derive L⊢CL \vdash CL⊢C.

Hint: From Part 2(c), you have L⊢□λ→□CL \vdash \Box\lambda \to \Box CL⊢□λ→□C. Chain this with the assumption L⊢□C→CL \vdash \Box C \to CL⊢□C→C to get L⊢□λ→CL \vdash \Box\lambda \to CL⊢□λ→C. Now compare this with what λ\lambdaλ says about itself.

Remark (The Santa Claus paradox and what Lob adds beyond Godel).

The Lobian sentence λ↔(□λ→C)\lambda \leftrightarrow (\Box\lambda \to C)λ↔(□λ→C) is a formal analogue of the Santa Claus sentence (also known as Curry's paradox). Consider the sentence SSS: "If this sentence is true, then Santa Claus exists." Let us try to determine whether SSS is true or false.

Well, SSS is an "if ... then ..." statement, so to check whether it is true, let us assume the "if" part and see whether the "then" part follows. So assume SSS is true. Since SSS says "if SSS is true then Santa Claus exists," and we are assuming SSS is true, it follows that Santa Claus exists. We have therefore shown: if SSS is true, then Santa Claus exists. But that is exactly what SSS says! So SSS is true. And since SSS is true and SSS implies Santa Claus exists, Santa Claus exists. Since nothing about this argument was specific to Santa Claus, the same reasoning "proves" any statement whatsoever.

The reason LLL does not fall prey to this paradox is that LLL cannot form a sentence that refers to its own truth. (A fundamental result called Tarski's theorem shows that no sufficiently powerful formal system can define a truth predicate for itself.) What LLL can do is refer to its own provability: the predicate □φ\Box\varphi□φ is a legitimate statement within LLL. The Lobian sentence λ\lambdaλ therefore substitutes "provable" for "true," asserting "if I am provable, then CCC." The proof of Lob's theorem shows that this substitution is enough to force L⊢CL \vdash CL⊢C — but only when □C→C\Box C \to C□C→C is already assumed, not unconditionally.

This mirrors a pattern: replacing "true" with "provable" transforms semantic paradoxes into precise theorems. The liar's paradox ("this sentence is false") becomes Godel's sentence ("this sentence is not provable"), yielding the incompleteness theorems. The Santa Claus paradox ("if this sentence is true, then CCC") becomes the Lobian sentence ("if this sentence is provable, then CCC"), yielding Lob's theorem.

What Lob adds beyond Godel. Godel's second incompleteness theorem (Exercise 1) says that LLL cannot prove its own consistency. This is already a serious obstacle, but one might hope that consistency is a special case — perhaps LLL can still trust its proofs in less sweeping ways. Lob's theorem crushes this hope completely. It says that for any statement CCC, if LLL can prove "my provability of CCC implies CCC is true" (i.e. L⊢□C→CL \vdash \Box C \to CL⊢□C→C), then CCC was already provable. There are no statements, not for which LLL can assert "well, if I could prove this, it would be true" without already being able to prove them. LLL does not trust its own proofs until it has witnessed them directly.

This is what makes Lob's theorem, rather than Godel's, the fundamental obstacle for tiling agents. Recall the setup from Exercise 1: a parent agent A1A_{1}A1​ builds a child A0A_{0}A0​ that only takes actions it can prove to be safe. For A1A_{1}A1​ to trust A0A_{0}A0​, it needs to know that A0A_{0}A0​'s proofs track reality — that is, A1A_{1}A1​ needs □P→P\Box P \to P□P→P for the statements PPP that A0A_{0}A0​ might act on. Godel tells us A1A_{1}A1​ cannot prove A0A_{0}A0​'s system is consistent. But Lob tells us something far stronger: A1A_{1}A1​ cannot even trust A0A_{0}A0​'s system on a case-by-case basis. For any individual statement CCC, the only way LLL can derive "if my proof system proves CCC, then CCC is really true" is if CCC was already provable — in which case the trust was never needed in the first place.

Part 2(e). In a one-shot Prisoner's Dilemma, two players each choose to either cooperate (CCC) or defect (DDD). In this variant, instead of choosing directly, each player submits a program that receives the opponent's source code as input and outputs CCC or DDD. Consider the following agent, FairBot:

algorithm FairBot(opponent)\texttt{FairBot}(\text{opponent})FairBot(opponent):
Search for an LLL-proof that opponent(FairBot)=C\texttt{opponent}(\texttt{FairBot}) = Copponent(FairBot)=C.
if proof found then return CCC
else return DDD

In words: FairBot cooperates with an opponent if and only if it can find an LLL-proof that the opponent cooperates with FairBot. Note that FairBot is unexploitable: if LLL is sound (i.e. LLL only proves true statements), then FairBot never cooperates with an opponent that defects against it.

The interesting question is what happens when FairBot plays against itself. At first glance, both mutual cooperation and mutual defection seem like stable outcomes.

We use Necessitation (N) L⊢φ⇒L⊢□φL\proves\varphi\Rightarrow L\proves\bx\varphiL⊢φ⇒L⊢□φ, Distribution (K) L⊢□(φ→ψ)→(□φ→□ψ)L\proves\bx(\varphi\to\psi)\to(\bx\varphi\to\bx\psi)L⊢□(φ→ψ)→(□φ→□ψ), and the Lob condition (4) L⊢□φ→□□φL\proves\bx\varphi\to\bx\bx\varphiL⊢□φ→□□φ.

"ProofSeeker(φ)\PS(\varphi)ProofSeeker(φ) halts" is exactly □φ\bx\varphi□φ, and a halting run is finite, so by the bridge L⊢□φL\proves\bx\varphiL⊢□φ. □\square□

Exercise 3.3 (The Complete Class Theorem). The setup: decision-making under uncertainty. Imagine you must choose an action, but you don't know which environment you are in. There are finitely many actions A={a1,…,ak}\mathcal{A}= \{a_{1}, \ldots, a_{k}\}A={a1​,…,ak​} and finitely many possible environments Ω={ω1,…,ωn}\Omega = \{\omega_{1}, \ldots, \omega_{n}\}Ω={ω1​,…,ωn​}. If you take action aaa and the true environment turns out to be ω\omegaω, you receive a reward u(a,ω)∈Ru(a, \omega) \in \mathbb{R}u(a,ω)∈R.

Example. You are deciding whether to carry an umbrella (a1a_{1}a1​) or not (a2a_{2}a2​). The environment is either "rainy" (ω1\omega_{1}ω1​) or "sunny" (ω2\omega_{2}ω2​). The rewards might be:

ω1 (rain)ω2 (sun)a1 (umbrella)85a2 (no umbrella)210\begin{array}{c|cc}& \omega_1 \text{ (rain)} & \omega_2 \text{ (sun)} \\ \hline a_1 \text{ (umbrella)} & 8 & 5 \\ a_2 \text{ (no umbrella)} & 2 & 10\end{array}a1​ (umbrella)a2​ (no umbrella)​ω1​ (rain)82​ω2​ (sun)510​​

Decision rules. A decision rule δ=(λ1,…,λk)\delta = (\lambda_{1}, \ldots, \lambda_{k})δ=(λ1​,…,λk​) is a (possibly randomized) strategy: you play action aja_{j}aj​ with probability λj\lambda_{j}λj​, where λj≥0\lambda_{j} \geq 0λj​≥0 and ∑j=1kλj=1\sum_{j=1}^{k} \lambda_{j} = 1∑j=1k​λj​=1. A pure decision rule puts all its weight on a single action (e.g. "always carry the umbrella"). A mixed rule randomizes (e.g. "carry the umbrella with probability 0.70.70.7").

The reward of δ\deltaδ in environment ω\omegaω is the average reward under the randomization:

u(δ,ω)  :=  ∑j=1kλj u(aj,ω).u(\delta, \omega) \;:=\; \sum_{j=1}^{k} \lambda_{j}\, u(a_{j}, \omega).u(δ,ω):=j=1∑k​λj​u(aj​,ω).

Risk vectors and the risk set. To compare decision rules across all environments simultaneously, we package the rewards into a single vector. The risk vector of a decision rule δ\deltaδ is

r(δ)  =  (u(δ,ω1),  …,  u(δ,ωn))  ∈  Rn.r(\delta) \;=\; \bigl(u(\delta, \omega_{1}),\; \ldots,\; u(\delta, \omega_{n})\bigr) \;\in\; \mathbb{R}^{n}.r(δ)=(u(δ,ω1​),…,u(δ,ωn​))∈Rn.

Each coordinate records how well δ\deltaδ performs in one environment. In the umbrella example, r(a1)=(8,5)r(a_{1}) = (8, 5)r(a1​)=(8,5) and r(a2)=(2,10)r(a_{2}) = (2, 10)r(a2​)=(2,10).

The risk set R\mathcal{R}R is the set of all risk vectors achievable by some decision rule:

R  =  {∑j=1kλj r(aj)  :  λj≥0,  ∑j=1kλj=1}.\mathcal{R}\;=\; \Bigl\{\sum_{j=1}^{k} \lambda_{j}\, r(a_{j}) \;:\; \lambda_{j} \geq 0,\; \sum_{j=1}^{k} \lambda_{j} = 1\Bigr\}.R={j=1∑k​λj​r(aj​):λj​≥0,j=1∑k​λj​=1}.

Geometrically, R\mathcal{R}R is the convex hull of the pure-action risk vectors {r(a1),…,r(ak)}\{r(a_{1}), \ldots, r(a_{k})\}{r(a1​),…,r(ak​)}: the set of all weighted averages of these points.

Admissibility (not being dominated). A decision rule δ\deltaδ is admissible if there is no other rule δ′\delta'δ′ that does at least as well as δ\deltaδ in every environment and strictly better in at least one. If such a δ′\delta'δ′ exists, we say δ′\delta'δ′ dominates δ\deltaδ, and any rational agent should prefer δ′\delta'δ′ — after all, switching from δ\deltaδ to δ′\delta'δ′ never hurts and sometimes helps, regardless of which environment is the true one.

The Pareto frontier F⊆R\mathcal{F}\subseteq \mathcal{R}F⊆R is the set of risk vectors of all admissible decision rules. A pure action aja_{j}aj​ is Pareto-optimal if r(aj)∈Fr(a_{j}) \in \mathcal{F}r(aj​)∈F.

Bayesian expected utility. A different approach to decision-making is to assign a prior π=(π1,…,πn)\pi = (\pi_{1}, \ldots, \pi_{n})π=(π1​,…,πn​) representing your beliefs about how likely each environment is, where πi≥0\pi_{i} \geq 0πi​≥0 and ∑iπi=1\sum_{i} \pi_{i} = 1∑i​πi​=1. (For example, π=(0.3,0.7)\pi = (0.3, 0.7)π=(0.3,0.7) means you believe there is a 30%30\%30% chance of rain.) The expected utility of δ\deltaδ under π\piπ is the weighted average reward:

EU(δ,π)  :=  ∑i=1nπi u(δ,ωi)  =  π⋅r(δ).\mathrm{EU}(\delta, \pi) \;:=\; \sum_{i=1}^{n} \pi_{i}\, u(\delta, \omega_{i}) \;=\; \pi \cdot r(\delta).EU(δ,π):=i=1∑n​πi​u(δ,ωi​)=π⋅r(δ).

A decision rule δ\deltaδ is Bayes-optimal under π\piπ if it achieves the highest expected utility among all decision rules: EU(δ,π)≥EU(δ′,π)\mathrm{EU}(\delta, \pi) \geq \mathrm{EU}(\delta', \pi)EU(δ,π)≥EU(δ′,π) for all δ′\delta'δ′.

The theorem. These two approaches to rational decision-making — admissibility ("never use a dominated strategy") and Bayesian expected utility maximization ("assign beliefs and maximize average reward") — turn out to characterize exactly the same set of decision rules:

Theorem (Complete Class). Every admissible decision rule is Bayes-optimal under some prior π\piπ with πi>0\pi_{i} > 0πi​>0 for all iii. Conversely, every Bayes-optimal rule under such a prior is admissible.

In other words: the decision rules that survive the "no domination" criterion are precisely those that arise from maximizing expected utility under some set of beliefs that doesn't rule out any environment entirely. This is significant because admissibility is an extremely weak rationality requirement — it says only that you shouldn't use a strategy when a strictly better one is available — yet it already forces expected utility maximization.

Part 3(a). Show the following two facts:

  • (i) Any admissible decision rule δ=∑jλj aj\delta = \sum_{j} \lambda_{j}\, a_{j}δ=∑j​λj​aj​ places zero weight on dominated pure actions: λj=0\lambda_{j} = 0λj​=0 whenever aja_{j}aj​ is not Pareto-optimal. (In other words, the Pareto frontier F\mathcal{F}F is contained in the convex hull of the Pareto-optimal pure actions alone.) Hint: If δ\deltaδ places positive weight on a dominated pure action aja_{j}aj​, replace aja_{j}aj​ with the action that dominates it. Does the resulting rule dominate δ\deltaδ?
  • (ii) Every Bayes-optimal rule under a prior π\piπ with πi>0\pi_{i} > 0πi​>0 for all iii is admissible. Hint: If some δ′\delta'δ′ dominated δ\deltaδ, compare their expected utilities. What does πi>0\pi_{i} > 0πi​>0 ensure?

F  =  {∑l=1pμl r(ail)  :  μl≥0,  ∑l=1pμl=1}F \;=\; \Bigl\{\sum_{l=1}^{p} \mu_{l}\, r(a_{i_l}) \;:\; \mu_{l} \geq 0,\; \sum_{l=1}^{p} \mu_{l} = 1\Bigr\}F={l=1∑p​μl​r(ail​​):μl​≥0,l=1∑p​μl​=1}

for some subset of Pareto-optimal pure actions {ai1,…,aip}\{a_{i_1}, \ldots, a_{i_p}\}{ai1​​,…,aip​​}. Solution

Higher reward is better; δ′\delta'δ′ dominates δ\deltaδ if r(δ′)≥r(δ)r(\delta')\ge\rdr(δ′)≥r(δ) coordinatewise with strict inequality in some coordinate. r(δ)\rdr(δ) is linear in the mixing weights, R=conv⁡{r(a1),…,r(ak)}R=\operatorname{conv}\{r(a_{1}),\dots,r(a_{k})\}R=conv{r(a1​),…,r(ak​)}, and EU⁡(δ,π)=π⋅r(δ)\EU(\delta,\pi)=\pi\cdot\rdEU(δ,π)=π⋅r(δ).

Part 3(a)(i). An admissible δ=∑jλjaj\delta=\sum_{j}\lambda_{j} a_{j}δ=∑j​λj​aj​ puts λj=0\lambda_{j}=0λj​=0 on every non-Pareto-optimal (dominated) aja_{j}aj​.

and strict in coordinate i0i_{0}i0​ (since λj>0\lambda_{j}>0λj​>0). So δ^\hat\deltaδ^ dominates δ\deltaδ, contradicting admissibility. Hence λj=0\lambda_{j}=0λj​=0, i.e. F⊆conv⁡{Pareto-optimal pure actions}F\subseteq\operatorname{conv}\{\text{Pareto-optimal pure actions}\}F⊆conv{Pareto-optimal pure actions}. □\square□

since every term is ≥0\ge0≥0 and the i0i_{0}i0​ term is >0>0>0. This contradicts Bayes-optimality, so δ\deltaδ is admissible. □\square□

Part 3(b). For a face F={∑l=1pμl r(ail):μl≥0, ∑lμl=1}\mathcal{F}=\{\sum_{l=1}^{p}\mu_{l}\,r(a_{i_l}):\mu_{l}\ge0,\ \sum_{l}\mu_{l}=1\}F={∑l=1p​μl​r(ail​​):μl​≥0, ∑l​μl​=1} with vl:=r(ail)−r(ai1)v_{l}:=r(a_{i_l})-r(a_{i_1})vl​:=r(ail​​)−r(ai1​​) and H=span⁡{v2,…,vp}H=\operatorname{span}\{v_{2},\dots,v_{p}\}H=span{v2​,…,vp​}: HHH is exactly the set of directions tangent to F\mathcal{F}F.

Take x,x+h∈Fx,x+h\in\mathcal{F}x,x+h∈F, say x=∑lμlr(ail)x=\sum_{l}\mu_{l} r(a_{i_l})x=∑l​μl​r(ail​​) and x+h=∑lμl′r(ail)x+h=\sum_{l}\mu_{l}' r(a_{i_l})x+h=∑l​μl′​r(ail​​) with ∑lμl=∑lμl′=1\sum_{l}\mu_{l}=\sum_{l}\mu_{l}'=1∑l​μl​=∑l​μl′​=1. Then

h=∑l(μl′−μl) r(ail)=∑l≥2(μl′−μl) vl∈H,h=\sum_{l}(\mu_{l}'-\mu_{l})\,r(a_{i_l})=\sum_{l\ge2}(\mu_{l}'-\mu_{l})\,v_{l}\in H,h=l∑​(μl′​−μl​)r(ail​​)=l≥2∑​(μl′​−μl​)vl​∈H,

using ∑l(μl′−μl)=0\sum_{l}(\mu_{l}'-\mu_{l})=0∑l​(μl′​−μl​)=0 to eliminate the r(ai1)r(a_{i_1})r(ai1​​) term. Hence moving within F\mathcal{F}F requires h∈Hh\in Hh∈H. Conversely, from any relative-interior point (μl>0\mu_{l}>0μl​>0) every h∈Hh\in Hh∈H is realized: x+εh∈Fx+\varepsilon h\in\mathcal{F}x+εh∈F for small ε>0\varepsilon>0ε>0. So the tangent directions of F\mathcal{F}F are precisely HHH. □\square□

Part 3(c). Let π⊥H\pi\perp Hπ⊥H be normalized so πi>0\pi_{i}>0πi​>0 and ∑iπi=1\sum_{i}\pi_{i}=1∑i​πi​=1, and assume no point of RRR scores strictly higher under π\piπ than the points of F\mathcal{F}F.

Solution. (i) For x,x′∈Fx,x'\in\mathcal{F}x,x′∈F we have x−x′∈Hx-x'\in Hx−x′∈H by 3(b), so π⋅(x−x′)=0\pi\cdot(x-x')=0π⋅(x−x′)=0. Thus π⋅r(δ)\pi\cdot\rdπ⋅r(δ) equals a common value ccc for all δ\deltaδ with r(δ)∈F\rd\in\mathcal{F}r(δ)∈F.

(ii) Picture π\piπ as the outward normal of the supporting hyperplane {x:π⋅x=c}\{x:\pi\cdot x=c\}{x:π⋅x=c}: by assumption the whole risk set lies on the inner side, π⋅x≤c\pi\cdot x\le cπ⋅x≤c for all x∈Rx\in Rx∈R, touching the hyperplane exactly along the face F\mathcal{F}F. Fix any r(δ)∈F\rd\in\mathcal{F}r(δ)∈F (so EU⁡(δ,π)=c\EU(\delta,\pi)=cEU(δ,π)=c) and any other rule δ′\delta'δ′. The step from the face point r(δ)\rdr(δ) to r(δ′)∈Rr(\delta')\in Rr(δ′)∈R heads back into the risk set, i.e. against the outward normal, so its dot product with π\piπ is non-positive:

π⋅(r(δ′)−r(δ))≤0,equivalentlyEU⁡(δ′,π)≤EU⁡(δ,π).\pi\cdot\big(r(\delta')-\rd\big)\le 0,\qquad\text{equivalently}\qquad \EU(\delta',\pi)\le\EU(\delta,\pi).π⋅(r(δ′)−r(δ))≤0,equivalentlyEU(δ′,π)≤EU(δ,π).

Since this holds for every δ′\delta'δ′, each rule with r(δ)∈F\rd\in\mathcal{F}r(δ)∈F maximizes expected utility, i.e. is Bayes-optimal under π\piπ.

Conclusion. If δ\deltaδ is admissible then r(δ)∈F\rd\in Fr(δ)∈F lies on some face F\mathcal{F}F; the prior π\piπ built from F\mathcal{F}F has all πi>0\pi_{i}>0πi​>0 and, by (ii), makes δ\deltaδ Bayes-optimal. Conversely, by 3(a)(ii) every Bayes-optimal rule under a strictly positive prior is admissible. The two classes coincide. □\square□

Exercise 3.4 (The Do-Divergence Theorem). Motivation: optimization as steering. A useful way to think about what it means for an agent to be optimizing is that it reliably steers the world into a narrow set of outcomes — outcomes that would be extremely unlikely to arise out of any random process . A thermostat keeps a room at 20 ∘ C despite varying weather; a chess player steers toward checkmate despite the opponent's moves. In each case, the actual outcome is concentrated in a small region of possibility space, whereas without the agent's intervention, outcomes would be spread broadly.

This exercise makes that intuition precise in an information-theoretic setting. We will show that an agent's ability to concentrate outcomes ("steer") is bounded by the amount of information the agent extracts from its observations.

Background: KL divergence. Given two probability distributions ppp and qqq over the same set of outcomes, the Kullback–Leibler (KL) divergence from qqq to ppp is

DKL(p ∥ q)  :=  ∑xp(x)log⁡p(x)q(x).D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p \,\|\, q) \;:=\; \sum_{x} p(x) \log \frac{p(x)}{q(x)}.DKL​(p∥q):=x∑​p(x)logq(x)p(x)​.

This quantity is always ≥0\geq 0≥0, and equals 000 only when p=qp = qp=q. It measures how "different" ppp is from qqq, with a particular asymmetry: DKL(p∥q)D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p \| q)DKL​(p∥q) is large when ppp places significant probability on outcomes where qqq assigns very little. In other words, it is large precisely when ppp concentrates on outcomes that would be surprising under qqq. This can be seen as a signature of optimization: the agent's policy makes certain outcomes likely that would be very unlikely under a baseline policy.

Background: mutual information. The mutual information between two random variables AAA and OOO is

MI(A; O)  :=  DKL(P[A,O] ∥ P[A] P[O])  =  ∑a,oP[a,o]log⁡P[a,o]P[a] P[o].\mathrm{MI}(A;\, O) \;:=\; D_{\mathrm{KL}}\bigl(P[A, O] \,\big\|\, P[A]\,P[O]\bigr) \;=\; \sum_{a, o}P[a, o] \log \frac{P[a, o]}{P[a]\,P[o]}.MI(A;O):=DKL​(P[A,O]​P[A]P[O])=a,o∑​P[a,o]logP[a]P[o]P[a,o]​.

This measures how much knowing OOO tells you about AAA (and vice versa). It is zero when AAA and OOO are independent, and large when they are tightly coupled.

Setup. Consider an agent (the "demon") that observes some information OOO about the world and then takes an action AAA based on what it observed. The action and observation together produce an outcome XXX. The joint distribution is

P[X,A,O]  =  P[X∣A,O]  P[A∣O]  P[O].P[X, A, O] \;=\; P[X \mid A, O]\; P[A \mid O]\; P[O].P[X,A,O]=P[X∣A,O]P[A∣O]P[O].

The factor P[A∣O]P[A \mid O]P[A∣O] encodes the demon's policy: how it chooses actions as a function of its observations.

Now consider a blind baseline: the demon still acts, but ignores its observations, choosing actions independently of OOO. We write the blind baseline distribution as

P[X,A,O∣do(A)]  =  P[X∣A,O]  P[A]  P[O].P[X, A, O \mid do(A)] \;=\; P[X \mid A, O]\; P[A]\; P[O].P[X,A,O∣do(A)]=P[X∣A,O]P[A]P[O].

The notation do(A)do(A)do(A) means we have "intervened" on the action, replacing the demon's observation-dependent policy P[A∣O]P[A \mid O]P[A∣O] with the marginal P[A]P[A]P[A] (the overall frequency of each action, ignoring which observations prompted them). The mechanism P[X∣A,O]P[X \mid A, O]P[X∣A,O] by which actions and observations produce outcomes is unchanged — only the demon's strategy has been lobotomized.

The theorem. Prove the Do-Divergence Theorem:

DKL(P[X] ∥ P[X∣do(A)])  ≤  MI(A; O).D_{\mathrm{KL}}\bigl(P[X] \,\big\|\, P[X \mid do(A)]\bigr) \;\leq\; \mathrm{MI}(A;\, O).DKL​(P[X]​P[X∣do(A)])≤MI(A;O).

The left side measures how much the sighted demon's outcome distribution differs from the blind baseline's. In the language of steering: it measures how much the demon has concentrated outcomes into regions that would be unlikely without observation-dependent action. The right side is the mutual information between actions and observations — how much the demon's actions depend on what it sees. The theorem says that the degree of steering is bounded by the information the demon uses.

Useful fact:

  • Monotonicity of KL divergence. For any two joint distributions p(x,y)p(x,y)p(x,y) and q(x,y)q(x,y)q(x,y), marginalizing out yyy can only decrease KL divergence: DKL(p(x) ∥ q(x))≤DKL(p(x,y) ∥ q(x,y))D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p(x) \,\|\, q(x)) \leq D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p(x,y) \,\|\, q(x,y))DKL​(p(x)∥q(x))≤DKL​(p(x,y)∥q(x,y)). (Intuitively: forgetting information can only make two distributions look more similar, never less.)

Hint: Compute DKL(P[X,A,O] ∥ P[X,A,O∣do(A)])D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P[X, A, O] \,\|\, P[X, A, O \mid do(A)])DKL​(P[X,A,O]∥P[X,A,O∣do(A)]) by expanding the log ratio using the factorizations above

Remark (Maxwell's demon and the thermodynamics of optimization).

Maxwell's demon is a thought experiment in which a tiny intelligent being controls a door between two halves of a box of gas. By observing each molecule's position and selectively opening the door, the demon can sort all molecules to one side, creating a highly ordered (low-entropy) state from an initially disordered one. In our notation: the outcome XXX is the final configuration of molecules, the observations OOO are the demon's measurements of molecular positions, and the actions AAA are its door openings.

Under the blind baseline (opening the door at random), molecules are roughly equally likely to be on either side, so P[X∣do(A)]P[X \mid do(A)]P[X∣do(A)] is spread broadly. If the demon perfectly sorts all nnn molecules to the right, P[X]P[X]P[X] is concentrated on a single configuration, and the KL divergence between these distributions is nlog⁡2n \log 2nlog2 (i.e. nnn bits). The theorem therefore says that perfectly sorting nnn molecules requires MI(A;O)≥n\mathrm{MI}(A; O) \geq nMI(A;O)≥n bits: the demon must gather at least nnn bits of information about the molecules to reduce the gas's entropy by nnn bits. This illustrates the idea that any agent that steers a system into a narrow, unlikely region of outcome space (low entropy) must pay for this steering with mutual information.

Solution

Write Pr⁡[X,A,O]=Pr⁡[X∣A,O]Pr⁡[A∣O]Pr⁡[O]\Pr[X,A,O]=\Pr[X\mid A,O]\Pr[A\mid O]\Pr[O]Pr[X,A,O]=Pr[X∣A,O]Pr[A∣O]Pr[O] and the blind baseline Pr⁡[X,A,O∣do(A)]=Pr⁡[X∣A,O]Pr⁡[A]Pr⁡[O]\Pr[X,A,O\mid\doo{A}]=\Pr[X\mid A,O]\Pr[A]\Pr[O]Pr[X,A,O∣do(A)]=Pr[X∣A,O]Pr[A]Pr[O].

Claim. DKL ⁣(Pr⁡[X] ∥ Pr⁡[X∣do(A)])≤MI⁡(A;O)\DKL\!\big(\Pr[X]\,\big\|\,\Pr[X\mid\doo{A}]\big)\le\MI(A;O)DKL​(Pr[X]​Pr[X∣do(A)])≤MI(A;O).

Solution. Compute the divergence between the full joints. The factors Pr⁡[X∣A,O]\Pr[X\mid A,O]Pr[X∣A,O] and Pr⁡[O]\Pr[O]Pr[O] cancel in the log-ratio:

DKL ⁣(Pr⁡[X,A,O] ∥ Pr⁡[X,A,O∣do(A)])=∑x,a,oPr⁡[x,a,o]log⁡Pr⁡[a∣o]Pr⁡[a].\DKL\!\big(\Pr[X,A,O]\,\big\|\,\Pr[X,A,O\mid\doo{A}]\big) =\sum_{x,a,o}\Pr[x,a,o]\log\frac{\Pr[a\mid o]}{\Pr[a]}.DKL​(Pr[X,A,O]​Pr[X,A,O∣do(A)])=x,a,o∑​Pr[x,a,o]logPr[a]Pr[a∣o]​.

The summand depends only on a,oa,oa,o; marginalizing xxx and using Pr⁡[a∣o]/Pr⁡[a]=Pr⁡[a,o]/(Pr⁡[a]Pr⁡[o])\Pr[a\mid o]/\Pr[a]=\Pr[a,o]/(\Pr[a]\Pr[o])Pr[a∣o]/Pr[a]=Pr[a,o]/(Pr[a]Pr[o]),

=∑a,oPr⁡[a,o]log⁡Pr⁡[a,o]Pr⁡[a]Pr⁡[o]=MI⁡(A;O).=\sum_{a,o}\Pr[a,o]\log\frac{\Pr[a,o]}{\Pr[a]\Pr[o]}=\MI(A;O).=a,o∑​Pr[a,o]logPr[a]Pr[o]Pr[a,o]​=MI(A;O).

Marginalizing the two joints down to XXX sends them to Pr⁡[X]\Pr[X]Pr[X] and Pr⁡[X∣do(A)]=∑a,oPr⁡[X∣a,o]Pr⁡[a]Pr⁡[o]\Pr[X\mid\doo{A}]=\sum_{a,o}\Pr[X\mid a,o]\Pr[a]\Pr[o]Pr[X∣do(A)]=∑a,o​Pr[X∣a,o]Pr[a]Pr[o] respectively, so monotonicity of KL under marginalization gives

DKL ⁣(Pr⁡[X] ∥ Pr⁡[X∣do(A)])≤DKL ⁣(Pr⁡[X,A,O] ∥ Pr⁡[X,A,O∣do(A)])=MI⁡(A;O).\DKL\!\big(\Pr[X]\,\big\|\,\Pr[X\mid\doo{A}]\big)\le\DKL\!\big(\Pr[X,A,O]\,\big\|\,\Pr[X,A,O\mid\doo{A}]\big)=\MI(A;O).DKL​(Pr[X]​Pr[X∣do(A)])≤DKL​(Pr[X,A,O]​Pr[X,A,O∣do(A)])=MI(A;O).

Exercise 3.5 (Channel Additivity). Consider two independent channels X1→Y1X_{1} \to Y_{1}X1​→Y1​ and X2→Y2X_{2} \to Y_{2}X2​→Y2​ with a fixed joint channel

P[Y∣X]  =  P[Y1∣X1] P[Y2∣X2].P[Y \mid X] \;=\; P[Y_{1} \mid X_{1}]\, P[Y_{2} \mid X_{2}].P[Y∣X]=P[Y1​∣X1​]P[Y2​∣X2​].

That is, output Y1Y_{1}Y1​ depends only on input X1X_{1}X1​, and Y2Y_{2}Y2​ depends only on X2X_{2}X2​; the two channels do not interact. We are free to choose the input distribution P[X]P[X]P[X] (which may correlate X1X_{1}X1​ and X2X_{2}X2​), and the joint distribution over everything is then P[Y,X]=P[Y∣X] P[X]P[Y, X] = P[Y \mid X]\, P[X]P[Y,X]=P[Y∣X]P[X]. The goal is to maximize the mutual information MI(X; Y)\mathrm{MI}(X;\, Y)MI(X;Y), called the information throughput of the channel.

Part 5(a). Show that for any input distribution P[X]P[X]P[X],

MI(X; Y)  =  MI(X1; Y1)  +  MI(X2; Y2)  −  MI(Y1; Y2).\mathrm{MI}(X;\, Y) \;=\; \mathrm{MI}(X_{1};\, Y_{1}) \;+\; \mathrm{MI}(X_{2};\, Y_{2}) \;-\; \mathrm{MI}(Y_{1};\, Y_{2}).MI(X;Y)=MI(X1​;Y1​)+MI(X2​;Y2​)−MI(Y1​;Y2​).

Hint: Write each mutual information as a KL divergence between the joint and the product of marginals, expand the log ratios using the channel factorization, and collect terms.

Part 5(b). Given any input distribution P[X1,X2]P[X_{1}, X_{2}]P[X1​,X2​], define

Q[X1,X2]  :=  P[X1] P[X2],Q[X_{1}, X_{2}] \;:=\; P[X_{1}]\, P[X_{2}],Q[X1​,X2​]:=P[X1​]P[X2​],

i.e. the product of the marginals. Show that MIQ(X; Y)≥MIP(X; Y)\mathrm{MI}_{Q}(X;\, Y) \geq \mathrm{MI}_{P}(X;\, Y)MIQ​(X;Y)≥MIP​(X;Y).

Hint: Under QQQ, the inputs are independent. What happens to MI(Y1; Y2)\mathrm{MI}(Y_{1};\, Y_{2})MI(Y1​;Y2​) when X1⊥ ⁣ ⁣ ⁣⊥X2X_{1} \perp\!\!\!\perp X_{2}X1​⊥⊥X2​, given the channel factorization? Use Part 5(a).

Part 5(c). Use Part 5(b) to conclude that there always exists a throughput-maximizing input distribution under which X1⊥ ⁣ ⁣ ⁣⊥X2X_{1} \perp\!\!\!\perp X_{2}X1​⊥⊥X2​.

Remark. This result has a natural interpretation in terms of optimization and agency. Think of XXX as the actions of an agent and YYY as the outcomes it cares about. The channel P[Y∣X]P[Y \mid X]P[Y∣X] — how actions influence outcomes — is fixed by the environment and outside the agent's control; the agent only gets to choose its policy P[X]P[X]P[X]. The factorization condition on P[Y∣X]P[Y \mid X]P[Y∣X] says that the environment is modular: the two groups of outcomes Y1Y_{1}Y1​ and Y2Y_{2}Y2​ are each influenced only by their respective actions X1X_{1}X1​ and X2X_{2}X2​. Our theorem says that if the environment is modular in this sense, then the agent can always find an optimal policy that is modular in a corresponding sense — specifically, the two groups of actions need not be coordinated at all and can be chosen independently.

Solution

The channel factorizes as P[Y∣X]=P[Y1∣X1]P[Y2∣X2]P[Y\mid X]=P[Y_{1}\mid X_{1}]P[Y_{2}\mid X_{2}]P[Y∣X]=P[Y1​∣X1​]P[Y2​∣X2​], and P[Y,X]=P[Y∣X]P[X]P[Y,X]=P[Y\mid X]P[X]P[Y,X]=P[Y∣X]P[X].

Part 5(a). MI⁡(X;Y)=MI⁡(X1;Y1)+MI⁡(X2;Y2)−MI⁡(Y1;Y2)\MI(X;Y)=\MI(X_{1};Y_{1})+\MI(X_{2};Y_{2})-\MI(Y_{1};Y_{2})MI(X;Y)=MI(X1​;Y1​)+MI(X2​;Y2​)−MI(Y1​;Y2​).

Solution. Using P[x,y]=P[y∣x]P[x]P[x,y]=P[y\mid x]P[x]P[x,y]=P[y∣x]P[x] and the factorization,

MI⁡(X;Y)=∑x,yP[x,y]log⁡P[y∣x]P[y]=∑x,yP[x,y]log⁡P[y1∣x1]P[y2∣x2]P[y1,y2].\MI(X;Y)=\sum_{x,y}P[x,y]\log\frac{P[y\mid x]}{P[y]}=\sum_{x,y}P[x,y]\log\frac{P[y_{1}\mid x_{1}]P[y_{2}\mid x_{2}]}{P[y_{1},y_{2}]}.MI(X;Y)=x,y∑​P[x,y]logP[y]P[y∣x]​=x,y∑​P[x,y]logP[y1​,y2​]P[y1​∣x1​]P[y2​∣x2​]​.

The three terms on the right are, respectively,

MI⁡(X1;Y1)=∑P[x,y]log⁡P[y1∣x1]P[y1],MI⁡(X2;Y2)=∑P[x,y]log⁡P[y2∣x2]P[y2],\MI(X_{1};Y_{1})=\sum P[x,y]\log\tfrac{P[y_1\mid x_1]}{P[y_1]},\quad \MI(X_{2};Y_{2})=\sum P[x,y]\log\tfrac{P[y_2\mid x_2]}{P[y_2]},MI(X1​;Y1​)=∑P[x,y]logP[y1​]P[y1​∣x1​]​,MI(X2​;Y2​)=∑P[x,y]logP[y2​]P[y2​∣x2​]​,MI⁡(Y1;Y2)=∑P[x,y]log⁡P[y1,y2]P[y1]P[y2],\MI(Y_{1};Y_{2})=\sum P[x,y]\log\tfrac{P[y_1,y_2]}{P[y_1]P[y_2]},MI(Y1​;Y2​)=∑P[x,y]logP[y1​]P[y2​]P[y1​,y2​]​,

each written over the full joint (the first depends only on x1,y1x_{1},y_{1}x1​,y1​, etc.). Then

MI⁡(X1;Y1)+MI⁡(X2;Y2)−MI⁡(Y1;Y2)=∑x,yP[x,y]log⁡P[y1∣x1]P[y2∣x2]P[y1,y2]=MI⁡(X;Y).□\MI(X_{1};Y_{1})+\MI(X_{2};Y_{2})-\MI(Y_{1};Y_{2}) =\sum_{x,y}P[x,y]\log\frac{P[y_{1}\mid x_{1}]P[y_{2}\mid x_{2}]}{P[y_{1},y_{2}]}=\MI(X;Y). \qedMI(X1​;Y1​)+MI(X2​;Y2​)−MI(Y1​;Y2​)=x,y∑​P[x,y]logP[y1​,y2​]P[y1​∣x1​]P[y2​∣x2​]​=MI(X;Y).□

Part 5(b). For Q[X1,X2]:=P[X1]P[X2]Q[X_{1},X_{2}]:=P[X_{1}]P[X_{2}]Q[X1​,X2​]:=P[X1​]P[X2​], MI⁡Q(X;Y)≥MI⁡P(X;Y)\MI_{Q}(X;Y)\ge\MI_{P}(X;Y)MIQ​(X;Y)≥MIP​(X;Y).

Solution. QQQ keeps the marginals Q[Xi]=P[Xi]Q[X_{i}]=P[X_{i}]Q[Xi​]=P[Xi​] and the channel, so MI⁡Q(Xi;Yi)=MI⁡P(Xi;Yi)\MI_{Q}(X_{i};Y_{i})=\MI_{P}(X_{i};Y_{i})MIQ​(Xi​;Yi​)=MIP​(Xi​;Yi​) for i=1,2i=1,2i=1,2 (MI⁡(Xi;Yi)\MI(X_{i};Y_{i})MI(Xi​;Yi​) depends only on P[Xi]P[X_{i}]P[Xi​] and P[Yi∣Xi]P[Y_{i}\mid X_{i}]P[Yi​∣Xi​]). Under QQQ the inputs are independent, so the outputs are too:

Q[y1,y2]=∑x1,x2Q[x1]Q[x2]P[y1∣x1]P[y2∣x2]=Q[y1] Q[y2],Q[y_{1},y_{2}]=\sum_{x_1,x_2}Q[x_{1}]Q[x_{2}]P[y_{1}\mid x_{1}]P[y_{2}\mid x_{2}]=Q[y_{1}]\,Q[y_{2}],Q[y1​,y2​]=x1​,x2​∑​Q[x1​]Q[x2​]P[y1​∣x1​]P[y2​∣x2​]=Q[y1​]Q[y2​],

hence MI⁡Q(Y1;Y2)=0\MI_{Q}(Y_{1};Y_{2})=0MIQ​(Y1​;Y2​)=0. Applying 5(a) under each distribution,

MI⁡Q(X;Y)=MI⁡P(X1;Y1)+MI⁡P(X2;Y2)=MI⁡P(X;Y)+MI⁡P(Y1;Y2)≥MI⁡P(X;Y),\MI_{Q}(X;Y)=\MI_{P}(X_{1};Y_{1})+\MI_{P}(X_{2};Y_{2}) =\MI_{P}(X;Y)+\MI_{P}(Y_{1};Y_{2})\ge\MI_{P}(X;Y),MIQ​(X;Y)=MIP​(X1​;Y1​)+MIP​(X2​;Y2​)=MIP​(X;Y)+MIP​(Y1​;Y2​)≥MIP​(X;Y),

the last step using MI⁡P(Y1;Y2)≥0\MI_{P}(Y_{1};Y_{2})\ge0MIP​(Y1​;Y2​)≥0. □\square□

Part 5(c). A throughput-maximizing input with X1⊥X2X_{1}\perp X_{2}X1​⊥X2​ always exists.

Solution. The input simplex is compact and MI⁡(X;Y)\MI(X;Y)MI(X;Y) continuous, so a maximizer P∗P^{*}P∗ exists. Let Q∗:=P∗[X1]P∗[X2]Q^{*}:=P^{*}[X_{1}]P^{*}[X_{2}]Q∗:=P∗[X1​]P∗[X2​]. By 5(b), MI⁡Q∗(X;Y)≥MI⁡P∗(X;Y)=max⁡\MI_{Q^*}(X;Y)\ge\MI_{P^*}(X;Y)=\maxMIQ∗​(X;Y)≥MIP∗​(X;Y)=max, so Q∗Q^{*}Q∗ is also a maximizer, and under Q∗Q^{*}Q∗ the inputs are independent. □\square□
